findings.title: Team administrators and owners are incorrectly denied access
findings.body: The authorization flag requires `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. Team roles are distinct, so a normal team administrator is not an owner and a normal owner is not an administrator; neither can satisfy this condition unless the helper methods deliberately overlap. This makes the advertised team-admin/owner access path unusable for bookings they do not personally organize or attend. Use an OR between the role checks.

findings.title: Guest blacklist can be bypassed by email casing
findings.body: Blacklist entries are normalized to lowercase, but submitted guest addresses are compared without normalization. Since valid email addresses may contain uppercase characters, submitting `Blocked@Example.com` bypasses a blacklist entry for `blocked@example.com` and creates/sends an invitation to that address. Normalize submitted addresses (and attendee duplicate comparisons) before applying policy checks.

findings.title: The API accepts duplicate guests and can fail or create duplicate attendees
findings.body: Duplicate validation exists only in the dialog, while the public tRPC schema and handler do not deduplicate `guests`. `uniqueGuests` only excludes attendees that existed before the request, so a direct request such as `["guest@example.com", "guest@example.com"]` retains both entries and passes both to `createMany`. Depending on the database constraint this either produces duplicate attendee rows and notifications or fails the whole mutation with a database error. Validate/deduplicate on the server before writing.

findings.title: Guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, or pending bookings through the API
findings.body: The handler updates any booking ID after authorization and never checks booking status or whether the event is still active. Although the list UI only exposes edit actions for accepted bookings, callers can invoke this mutation directly for cancelled/rejected/pending (and past) bookings. It then adds attendee records and sends calendar `REQUEST`/confirmed emails for an event that may no longer exist. Enforce the allowed booking state server-side before modifying attendees.

findings.title: Existing attendees can receive a new-booking email when mixed with new guests
findings.body: The database write correctly filters `guests` into `uniqueGuests`, but notifications are called with the original `guests` array. If a request contains both an already-attending address and a new address, `sendAddGuestsEmails` classifies the existing attendee as a newly added guest and sends it an `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (including a calendar invite) instead of the guest-added update. Pass `uniqueGuests` to the mail sender.

findings.title: Guest list size is unbounded
findings.body: The mutation accepts an unbounded array of email addresses. Any authorized attendee can submit a very large payload, causing an equally large database insert, calendar attendee update, and email fan-out; the latter also sends update emails to every existing attendee. This is an application-level mail/third-party API abuse vector and can exhaust request resources. Add a server-side maximum guest count (and ideally a matching UI limit).

findings.title: Guest-add notifications ignore event-type email opt-out settings
findings.body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` sends organizer, team-member, existing-attendee, and new-attendee emails unconditionally. Other standard booking notification paths check `disableStandardEmails.all.host` and `.attendee`, but this new path neither accepts event metadata nor performs those checks. Consequently, adding a guest overrides an event type's configured host/attendee email suppression and sends notifications users explicitly disabled.
